''Long Columns and Struts: Compression and Bending.''—A long strut or pillar, compressed by forces <math>\text{P}</math> applied at the ends in the direction of the axis, becomes unstable as regards flexure when <math>\text{P}</math> exceeds a certain value. Under no circumstances can this value of <math>\text{P}</math> be exceeded in loading a strut. But it may happen that the intensity of stress produced by smaller loads exceeds the safe compressive strength of the material, in which case a lower limit of load must be chosen. If the applied load is not strictly axial, if the strut is not initially straight, if it is subject to any deflexion by transverse forces, or if the modulus of elasticity is not uniform over each cross-section—then loads smaller than the limit which causes instability will produce a certain deflexion which increases with increase of load, and will give rise to a uniformly varying stress of the kind illustrated in figs. 28 and 30. We shall first consider the ideal case in which the forces at the ends are strictly axial, the strut perfectly straight and free from transverse loads and perfectly symmetrical as to elasticity. Two conditions have to be distinguished—that in which the ends are held by pins or sockets which leave them free to rock, and that in which the ends are held fixed. Suppose in the first place that the ends are free to rock. The value of the load which causes instability will be found by considering what force <math>\text{P}</math> applied to each end would suffice to hold an originally straight strut in a bent state, supposing it to have received a small amount of elastic curvature in any way. It is shown by Euler that the force required to maintain the strut in its curved state is <math>\text{P} = \pi^2\text{EI}/\text{L}^2</math>, and is independent of the deflexion. This means that with this particular value of <math>\text{P}</math> (which for brevity we shall write <math>\text{P}_1</math>) the strut will be in neutral
readings.c2s2:
equilibrium when bent; with a value of <math>\text{P}</math> less than <math>\text{P}_1</math> it will be stable; with a greater value it will be unstable. Hence a load exceeding <math>\text{P}_1</math> will certainly cause rupture. The value <math>\pi^2\text{EI}/\text{L}^2</math> applies to struts with ends free to rock. If the ends are fixed the effective length for bending is reduced by one half, so that <math>\text{P}_1</math> then is <math>4\pi^2\text{EI}/\text{L}^2</math>. When one end is fixed and the other is free to rock <math>\text{P}_1</math> has an intermediate value, probably about <math>9\pi^2\text{EI}/4\text{L}^2</math>.

The above theory assigns <math>\text{P}_1</math> as a limit to the strength of a strut on account of flexural instability; but a stress less than <math>\text{P}_1</math> may cause direct crushing. Let <math>\text{S}</math> be the area of section, and <math>f_c</math> the strength of the material to resist crushing. Thus a strut which conforms to the ideal conditions specified above will fail by simple crushing if <math>f_c\text{S}</math> is less than <math>\text{P}_1</math>, but by bending if <math>f_c\text{S}</math> is greater than <math>\text{P}_1</math>. Hence with a given material and form of section the ideal strut will fail by direct crushing if the length is less than a certain multiple of the least breadth (easily calculated from the expression for <math>\text{P}_1</math>), and in that case its strength will be independent of the length; when the length is greater than this the strut will yield by bending, and its strength diminishes rapidly as the length is increased.

But the conditions which the above theory assumes are never realized in practice. The load is never strictly axial, nor the strut absolutely straight to begin with, nor the elasticity uniform. The result is that the strength is in all cases less than either <math>f_c\text{S}</math> or <math>\text{P}_1</math>, and the results of experiments are best expressed by means of a formula, which is in part empirical, giving continuous values for struts of any length. For very short struts we have seen that the ideal breaking load is <math>f_c\text{S}</math>, and for very long struts it is <math>\pi^2\text{EI}/\text{L}^2</math>. If we write <math>\text{P} = f_c\text{S}/(1 + f_c\text{SL}^2/\pi^2\text{EI})</math>, we have a formula which gives correct values in these two extreme cases, and intermediate values for struts

For fixed ends <math>\tfrac{1}{4}c</math> is to be taken in place of <math>c</math>.
